rv.q: Smart, funny, splendid to look at and all with a beat you can dance to, this tribute to the Brothers Grimm, the sisters of the Second Wave and, not least, the indomitable Ms. Spears, is a delight.
This jukebox musical built around Britney Spears songs is a colorful, energetic and surprisingly sweet confection that delivers exactly what it promises.

In the end cooler heads prevail and equity reigns supreme, albeit with a too-neatly wrapped bow around a complex problem. Tackling gender roles and power dynamics never sounded as good as it does in “Once Upon a One More Time,” in which Spears’ songs are diligently retro-fitted to the message without sounding jimmied into place.

Ms. Simard, seen before in “Company” and “Hello, Dolly!,” is one of Broadway’s unsung, or undersung, treasures, and her performance alone brings sufficient pleasure to make this trip to Britney-land worth a visit.
This timidity is but one example of the ways in which the show comes up short, both as a feminist text and as a tribute to Spears’s songbook — and, yes, her life.
The sillier and more turbo-charged the tribute, the better.
But the story, by another Broadway newbie, Jon Hartmere, aims for both impishness and profundity, with muddled results.
Once Upon a One More Time is a well-assembled and entertaining diversion.
Instead, it’s reductive and pandering, hitting all the expected marks without any unique spark.
The central flaw is a slipshod story that just doesn’t track
It’s bibbidi-bobbidi-brainless.
Only one Spears show on Broadway is truly “Toxic.”
Spears's hits and impeccable dancing from director/choreographers Keone and Mari Madrid make Once Upon a One More Time an irresistible party.

Once Upon a One More Time, which is being touted in attorney-speak as "fully authorized and licensed post-conservatorship by Grammy Award-winning pop icon Britney Spears," is a surprisingly tasty treat, both for the eyes and for the ears.

Once Upon a One More Time is a jukebox musical that takes fairy tale princesses and gives them a feminist awakening through the pop hits of Britney Spears. The result is a show that's earnest in its messaging but uneven in its execution.
Once Upon a One More Time is a youthful, exuberant take on beloved tales that's more dazzling and polished than Cinderella's glass slipper.
Go to have fun, not to ponder the meaning of existence.

If “Once Upon a One More Time,” opening at Broadway’s Theater tonight, is clearly not strikingly original, the story does have a few distinctive touches, and the production Broadway-level pleasures. The design is flashy, and the choreography is thrilling.
On the other hand, hearing those two ladies – now played by Amy Hillner Larsen and Tess Soltai – sing “Work Bitch” is almost worth the price of admission.
It’s all a bit much, frankly, but then again, it’s not like anyone was expecting waltzes.
Let’s hope that her estate is being duly recompensed for the use of her personage, because her message has been perverted here into mere tokenism.
Once Upon a One More Time emerges as a worthwhile concept thwarted by poor execution.
It may entrance many of the Princess of Pops fans with all her most famous songs but it is the weakest of the five as a stage musical.
Her delivery of “Toxic” momentarily enlivens an otherwise lackluster second act.
But even for them, one sensed—given the audience responses—the musical hit big at some moments, but did not hit big throughout.
Once Upon a One More Time often feels sadly passé.
Derivative where it’s not baffling, and paper thin where it’s not derivative, Once Upon a One More Time can’t even pull off the baseline achievement of jukebox musicals: make the songs sound good.

While one might also add “Into the Woods” (which was just revived on Broadway and also combines characters from different fairy tales into a single plot) to the list of precedents, I would prefer to not compare that Sondheim masterwork with a piece of junk like “Once Upon a One More Time.”
The rest of this summer dud is just a pale and pandering whitewash.
As I sat in the audience, I found myself genuinely having a good time.
If you give it a chance, “A One More Time” is more entertaining than you’d expect.
For those simply looking for an energizing but ultimately forgettable night on Broadway, once might be enough for Once Upon a One More Time.
The show never takes itself seriously, as it sneaks in ironic jokes about the patriarchy.

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on this Britney Spears jukebox musical about feminist fairy tale princesses, with some enjoying its campy energy and others finding it derivative, heavy-handed, and a creative misfire.

sg.ra: The Marquis is the only Broadway house built entirely inside a hotel (3rd floor of the Marriott Marquis), so the orchestra was engineered from scratch in 1986 with a gentle continuous rake and no interior columns. Center Orchestra rows C-H deliver the theater's signature payoff: Portman designed every seat to be within 80 ft of the stage, so even at row F you are close enough to read faces, with none of the pre-war pillars or sightline quirks of older 46th Street houses. Aisle seats gain from the above-average legroom the hotel footprint allows.

Because the Marquis sits inside the hotel's structural envelope, the proscenium is 40 ft wide but wings are only 20 ft — half code. That unusually shallow stage means side-orchestra patrons lose less upstage action than they would at a wider house; what gets cut is limited to the far corner opposite your seat. Double-digit seats in the Right Orchestra are explicitly noted as giving partial views of the stage-right corner, so shows with heavy blocking at the edges (spectacle musicals) still work here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but it barely bites
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang technically begins at Orchestra row M, but multiple source guides agree the Marquis overhang is unusually forgiving — a quirk of the 1986 hotel-integrated design where Portman's 80-ft max-distance rule kept the balcony pulled forward but shallow. Reviewers consistently report the stage itself remains clearly visible even in the back rows, and the rear orchestra prices drop to a mid tier while you keep the same smooth rake. The real tradeoff here is detail/immersion, not obstruction. Accessible (Row Y) seating is in this zone via ramp.

sg.vl: Row A is a premium orchestra alternative
sg.ra: The Marquis mezzanine is the theater's signature asset: because the house was built fresh in 1986 inside the hotel shell rather than retrofitted, designers used true stadium stepping with a 'gap' between rows so the person in front of you does not block sightlines. Reviewers and Tripadvisor users repeatedly single out Row A Center Mezz as sometimes preferable to any orchestra seat — elevated, unobstructed, pulled forward by the 80-ft rule. Front-mezz single-digit seats deliver the sweeping view musicals are meant to be seen from.

The Marquis mezzanine only runs 12 rows deep (A-M, no I) — shallow by Broadway standards because the hotel footprint capped balcony depth. That means row H is still close to the stage by mezzanine math, and the stadium stepping holds all the way back. Rows H-K near center are flagged as good value across multiple guides: single-digit seats clear the rail, the elevated angle still suits musicals, and prices drop meaningfully versus rows A-D.

Two Marquis-specific drawbacks converge here. First, the NYTix venue guide notes 'rear mezz audio is sometimes a bit fuzzy as are the sight lines from this area' — consistent with BWW forum complaints that the Marquis has unusually dead natural acoustics because the carpeted hotel-interior walls absorb sound. Second, mezzanine access is stairs-only from the lobby (no elevator to this level), so the cheapest seats are also the hardest to reach. Far-side mezz seats additionally lose the corresponding stage corner.

vr.q: I actually think it's a really fun musical. And I think that Broadway needs more fun camping musicals.
if you want a good fun time out and you really love Britney Spears music and you wanna see some freaking amazing choreo, go see Once Upon One More Time

I also thought the book and the music arrangements were a little bit uneven, especially in terms of suiting the pop music to the more musical theatre voices. But I thought the choreo was amazing and I was thoroughly entertained.
